claims.text: Single-phase formation and crystal-structure selection in rapidly heated noble-metal HEA nanoparticles are controlled jointly by precursor mobility and cooling history.
Tailored organic-ligand binding limits precursor or atomic mobility during rapid heating.
An intermediate cooling hold at approximately 150–200 °C permits controlled, limited atomic rearrangement.
The limited rearrangement enabled by the intermediate hold prevents phase separation and elemental segregation.
A fixed equiatomic or near-equiatomic mixture of noble-metal salts such as Au, Pt, Pd, Rh, and Ir is an applicable precursor state.
Millisecond-scale rapid heating is an established processing regime for HEA nanoparticle formation.
The process forms homogenized nuclei whose coalescence depends on ligand-controlled mobility and thermal relaxation during cooling.
Organic ligands tether metal ions in the precursor.
Restricted atomic mobility can oppose interaction-driven structural preferences and favor a more mixed multielement nanoparticle.
An intermediate hold creates a narrow time window that corrects local compositional fluctuations without permitting extensive diffusion and segregation.
Combining ligand-imposed mobility restriction with programmed cooling kinetically traps a uniform single-phase solid solution.

Ligand-modified nanoparticles subjected to an intermediate cooling hold will show a more uniform single-phase structure and less elemental segregation than immediately quenched nanoparticles prepared without tailored ligands.
The selected single phase may be FCC or a similar crystal structure.
Ligand modification combined with an intermediate hold will lower the apparent decomposition temperature relative to the immediately quenched ligand-free baseline.
Immediate quenching without tailored ligands typically produces greater phase separation, elemental segregation, and poorer crystal-structure control.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble-metal HEA nanoparticles containing more than five elements under rapid thermal-shock synthesis.
The mechanism requires ligands that remain sufficiently stable at high temperature to modulate mobility without premature decomposition.
Element-specific mixing enthalpies can introduce preferences for particular structures.
Differences in metal–ligand interactions and mixing enthalpies may cause the proposed treatment to vary in effectiveness among compositions.
